"Countenance" is a formal, somewhat literary word. In its noun form, it carries two distinct meanings — one about a person's face, and one about approval or support. Both meanings are still used today, though you'll encounter them more in books, formal writing, or serious speech than in casual conversation.
Meaning 1: A Person's Face or Facial Expression

This is the more common meaning. When someone uses "countenance" to refer to a face, they don't just mean the physical structure — they almost always mean the expression on the face, the look it carries, the emotion it shows. Think of it as the face as a window to inner feeling.

Examples:

  • "His countenance darkened when he heard the bad news." — His expression turned grim.
  • "She had a kind, gentle countenance." — Her face wore a kind, gentle expression.
  • "The soldier kept a stern countenance throughout the ceremony." — The soldier's face showed no weakness or emotion.

Notice that in each example, the word is doing double duty — describing both the face and what that face is communicating. That's the beauty of this word. When a writer says someone's "countenance fell," you instantly know the face dropped into sadness. It's expressive in a compact way.

This meaning is less obvious but equally important. "Countenance" can also mean the active support, approval, or sanction you give to something — particularly something questionable or controversial.

Think of it this way: when a person in a position of authority or respect gives their "countenance" to something, they are lending it their approval. Their face, so to speak, is turned toward it favorably.

Examples:

  • "The king gave his countenance to the new law." — The king officially approved it.
  • "The school refused to give countenance to bullying of any kind." — The school refused to approve of or tolerate it.
  • "His presence at the meeting gave countenance to ideas he privately disagreed with." — His being there implied approval, even if he didn't actually agree.

This meaning often appears with the verbs give, lend, or refuse — as in "give countenance to," "lend countenance to," or "refuse to give countenance to."

"Keep one's countenance"
This means to keep your face under control — to hold back laughter, shock, or any strong emotion and stay composed.

  • "It was hard to keep his countenance when she tripped over the cat." — It was hard not to burst out laughing.

"Out of countenance"
To be "out of countenance" means to be visibly embarrassed, flustered, or caught off guard — your composure has been disrupted.

  • "The unexpected question put her completely out of countenance." — She was thrown off and looked visibly uncomfortable.

"Put someone out of countenance"
To embarrass or disconcert someone; to make them lose their composure.

  • "His rude remark put the whole room out of countenance."
How to Tell the Two Meanings Apart in Context

It's usually very easy. Ask yourself: Is the sentence talking about a person's face or expression? → Meaning 1. Is it talking about approval, support, or tolerance of something? → Meaning 2.

  • "She had a worried countenance." → Face/expression. ✓
  • "They refused to give countenance to violence." → Approval/support. ✓

"Countenance" belongs to a more elevated, formal register of English. You wouldn't say "Nice countenance, man" — that would sound bizarre. But in a novel, a speech, a legal document, or formal writing, it fits naturally. When you use it, it signals that you're choosing your words with care.

It also carries a certain dignity. Saying someone's "countenance fell" feels more weighty and human than simply saying "their face fell." The word invites you to picture not just a face, but a person — with all their inner life showing through.
One-Line Summaries to Lock It In

• Meaning 1: Your countenance is your face — especially the expression it wears.
  • Meaning 2: To give countenance to something is to give it your approval or support.
